page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.se1.4xlarge is a memory-optimized virtual instance built on KVM virtualization and powered by an x86_64 Intel Xeon 8269CY processor clocked at 2.5 GHz. The instance provisions 16 dedicated vCPUs mapped across 8 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading enabled. The CPU configuration includes 32 KB L1 data cache, 1.0 MB L2 cache, and a shared 35 MB L3 cache, along with instruction set extensions including AVX-512F, AES, and FMA. Memory capacity totals 128.0 GB, delivering a 1:8 core-to-memory ratio of 8.0 GB per vCPU. The instance does not include integrated local disk storage, requiring external network block storage volumes, and offers a baseline network bandwidth of 3 Gbps without hardware GPU acceleration.

Benchmark results demonstrate modest compute capabilities aligned with mid-tier enterprise hardware. Multi-core performance reaches middle-tier percentiles, reflected in a Geekbench multi-core score of 5755.0, a stress-ng multi-core rating of 11774.7, and a PassMark CPU score of 13059.36. Conversely, single-thread throughput is restrained, marked by a Geekbench single-core score of 933.0 and weak single-threaded compression speeds. Memory subsystem throughput records 76.43 GB/sec in large-block read operations and 55.34 GB/sec in large-block writes, though overall PassMark memory performance ranks in the lower quartile.

Hardware resource allocation is characterized by an asymmetry between expansive RAM density and limited networking and single-core compute. The 3 Gbps network baseline and absence of native NVMe storage restrict high-throughput local data ingest. However, the 128.0 GB RAM footprint coupled with steady multi-core execution supports caching and medium-scale memory residency efficiently without overprovisioning compute resources.

Alibaba Cloud ecs.se1.4xlarge is functionally suited for in-memory caching solutions like Redis, which sustained 11.3 million SET operations per second in testing. Additional viable workloads include medium-sized relational database replicas, in-memory data processing, static web application serving, and backend application tiers that depend on significant working memory rather than heavy per-core computational throughput.
